title: Renewable continuity
blurb: A recurring pattern followed through the five places where it does its clearest work.

steps.why: States the pattern: order emerges, a threat fractures it, right action restores it, and the work repeats.
Creation is the first instance of the pattern and never a finished event.
The sun performs the same restoration every night.
Kingship and ethics are the human share of the same maintenance.
Death poses the pattern at the scale of a single person.

title: From creation to daily temple service
blurb: How a cosmogony becomes a repeated morning routine performed by named officials.

steps.why: Local traditions describe how differentiated life began.
Explains why several accounts could stand at once without a winner.
The temple models the created world and re-enacts its maintenance daily.
Names the effective power the rite depends on.

title: Re through night and day
blurb: The solar circuit from sunset to sunrise, and the compositions that map it.

steps.why: The cycle in outline, with its forms of the sun.
The royal Underworld Books divide the night into hours and gates.
Locates the Duat among sky, west, water, and tomb without flattening them into one map.

title: Osiris, succession, death, and regeneration
blurb: A family conflict that carries kingship, mourning, and the afterlife.

steps.why: The core relationships and the conflict that drives them.
Set is not a constant villain; his reputation changes across periods.
Funeral ritual applies the Osirian pattern to ordinary dead.
Judgment and vindication complete the sequence for an individual.

title: Maat across ethics, kingship, and ritual
blurb: One word doing work in three registers.

steps.why: Defines the pair and the royal responsibility.
Turns maat into advice about listening, restraint, and speech.
Presenting maat is a physical offering in temple ritual.
The heart is weighed against maat at the threshold.

title: Body, name, ka, ba, and akh
blurb: Why 'soul' is the wrong translation, and what each aspect needed.

steps.why: The whole set and the problems each aspect solves.
Ritual addresses each aspect in a specific way.
Spells for integrity, mobility, and provisioning name these needs directly.

title: Nile, sacred geography, Sobek, and Hapi
blurb: Religion read from the shape of the land and the behaviour of the river.

steps.why: Orientation first: upstream is south, and the west belongs to the dead.
A deity whose range follows water, marsh, and royal patronage.
Takes the same geography to specific standing sites.

title: Pyramid Texts to Coffin Texts to Book of the Dead
blurb: Overlapping corpora, kept overlapping. The corpora overlap rather than forming a ladder.

steps.why: States why replacement is the wrong model.
The earliest surviving corpus, and the debate about what it was for.
Wider access, new media, continuing material.
Individual commissions that still reuse much older spells.

title: What religion does
blurb: A route through definitions, institutions, ritual, animals, and the limits of interpretation.
purpose: To give readers a working method for studying religion through Egypt without reducing it to belief, anxiety, or a list of gods.

steps.why: Sets out the questions and evidence needed before treating religion as a single object.
Connects texts, places, bodies, institutions, and practices without making one register stand for all religion.
Shows how built space, labor, access, and repeated offerings organize a public institution.
Tests ritual as a practical response to uncertain worlds without turning it into a clinical diagnosis.
Expands the method to animals, images, objects, and landscapes as relationships rather than symbols alone.
Returns to the evidence ladder and names the limits of analogy, diagnosis, and timeless claims.

leavesOut: This collection does not give a full chronology, a complete history of every deity, or a substitute for reading the primary texts and specialist scholarship.

title: How an early state formed
blurb: A comparative route through landscapes, regional cultures, writing, monuments, kingship, and the problem of 'civilization'.
purpose: To explain state formation as a set of material and political processes rather than as a race toward one universal model of civilization.

steps.why: Establishes the river, deserts, regional orientation, and places where power became visible.
Introduces regional cultures and the evidence for aggregation, hierarchy, and early political change.
Shows writing as a set of practices tied to knowledge, administration, and unequal access.
Connects monumental form to quarrying, logistics, work, and claims about state capacity.
Examines the moral and political language that presents rule as maintenance of order.
Uses comparison to sharpen questions about city, territory, writing, and power rather than to rank civilizations.

leavesOut: This collection does not reconstruct every Predynastic region, treat state formation as a single event, or make Egypt and Mesopotamia interchangeable cases.

title: Ritual, continuity, and uncertainty
blurb: A route from the archive's opening questions to heka, ritual change, renewal, misfortune, and death.
purpose: To ask what ritual makes possible when people face danger, loss, repetition, and outcomes they cannot control.

steps.why: Provides the archive's basic orientation and its warning against treating restoration as automatic success.
Names effective power and keeps healing, words, objects, and action together.
Makes uncertainty explicit and distinguishes repeated forms from claims of unbroken continuity.
Places permanence beside renewal and asks what continuity means in a changing world.
Keeps pain and ritual failure in view instead of ending every story with restored order.
Shows how rites address a final uncertainty through bodies, memory, offerings, and unequal access.

leavesOut: This collection does not diagnose ancient people, make ritual into anxiety management, or assume every rite worked as intended.

title: Permanence, suffering, and impermanence
blurb: A careful comparison of renewal, misfortune, early Buddhist analysis, personhood, and festival life.
purpose: To compare Egyptian and early Buddhist questions without turning permanence and impermanence into caricatures of whole cultures.

steps.why: Defines Egyptian permanence as an active process of renewal rather than simple stasis.
Tests ideals of order against pain, injustice, and the limits of restoration.
Introduces anicca, dukkha, and anatta as historically situated analytical terms, not civilizational labels.
Returns to Egyptian bodies, names, memory, and renewal at the scale of a person.
Brings comparison back to public movement, consultation, household practice, and uncertain outcomes.

leavesOut: This collection is not a survey of Buddhism or Egypt, and it does not claim direct transmission from one tradition to the other.

title: The afterlives of Egypt
blurb: A route through Greek and Roman transformations, biblical and Christian memory, museums, popular culture, and modern identity.
purpose: To treat the legacy of Egypt as a history of reception, adaptation, use, and contest rather than as a single surviving essence.

steps.why: Defines reception as something later people do with Egypt's materials, names, and images.
Shows adaptation and movement across languages, institutions, and imperial settings.
Separates biblical narrative and Christian memory from Egyptian historical evidence.
Keeps Coptic and Islamic histories inside Egypt's story rather than treating pharaonic time as its endpoint.
Examines collecting, classification, power, provenance, and the institutions that made knowledge portable.
Tracks reinvention in Egyptian Revival and popular media rather than calling every reuse a survival.
Ends with African, diasporic, and contemporary claims over who can narrate Egypt.

leavesOut: This collection does not offer a complete history of Coptic, Islamic, colonial, diasporic, or popular receptions. Each later setting needs its own sources and local histories.

title: Vulnerable bodies and practical care
blurb: A route through households, healing, heka, ritual uncertainty, suffering, and the dead.
purpose: To place bodily vulnerability, unequal access, illness, care, and grief at the center of religious history.

steps.why: Starts with the people and labor that elite archives often leave at the margins.
Treats remedies, incantations, objects, and practitioners as a porous field rather than a medicine versus magic binary.
Shows how words, materials, bodies, and action can be effective without fitting a modern clinical category.
Keeps failure, revision, and uncertainty visible in repeated practice.
Asks how people explain pain when order and justice do not line up.
Follows care through burial, memory, offerings, and the dignity due to human remains.

leavesOut: This collection does not diagnose ancient people, reduce disability to a symbol, or make one healing text representative of all Egyptian care.

title: Material and more-than-human religion
blurb: A route through river, animals, temples, monuments, offerings, and festivals as relationships made through matter.
purpose: To understand religion through bodies, substances, buildings, animals, landscapes, and repeated acts instead of treating material things as illustrations of belief.

steps.why: Sets the river, desert, horizon, and regional places in relation to religious action.
Separates iconography, manifestation, cult animals, and votive mummies.
Provides a comparative guide to forms, places, roles, and changes without flattening local gods into fixed types.
Follows materials, workers, logistics, and maintenance into the making of lasting forms.
Shows buildings as sensory and institutional environments maintained through repeated service.
Returns materials and bodies to public movement, consultation, and household practice.

leavesOut: This collection does not claim that every object has agency in the same sense, or that material evidence can recover the thoughts of people who used it.

title: Prepare for the Esna-to-Aswan journey
blurb: A reading route for the included cruise, from river orientation and layered temples to living communities, Nubia, and the trip guide.
purpose: To prepare a traveler to read the route with historical depth, attention to living communities, and a clear boundary between the included cruise and optional extensions.

steps.why: Establishes the route, the dahabiya as a modern vessel, and the changing river before any stop is treated as timeless.
Begins at embarkation with Khnum, late temple theology, conservation, craft, and the town's layered history.
Moves to walls, Nekhbet, provincial memory, tomb biography, and settlement evidence.
Pairs the standing Temple of Horus with Tell Edfu, ritual history, and conservation.
Follows sandstone extraction, inscriptions, shrines, transport, and the labor behind temple stone.
Prepares the paired temple and museum through Sobek, Harwer, animal relationships, and careful display ethics.
Frames household visits, farming, bread, fishing, markets, hospitality, consent, and reciprocity as contemporary life.
Places the unnamed community visit within Nubian plurality, Kushite history, dam displacement, and living identity.
Closes with the included route boundary, public places, optional extensions, and ways to keep reading after checkout.

leavesOut: This collection does not identify private hosts, map the unnamed Nubian town, guarantee optional activities, or turn contemporary visits into evidence of unchanged antiquity.

title: From first labels to the Latin alphabet
blurb: A transmission route from Early Dynastic labels through Egyptian phonetic practice, early alphabetic experiments, Phoenician, Greek, and Latin.
purpose: To explain how Egyptian writing already used one-consonant signs while keeping the later alphabetic transmission chain, its evidence, and its disputed links distinct.

steps.why: Places the earliest surviving Egyptian writing in tomb U-j, labels, royal cemetery evidence, and the limits of an archaeological context.
Defines one-consonant signs, rebus writing, biliterals, triliterals, determinatives, and the mixed system that remained useful.
Connects the Nile to the Western and Eastern Desert roads, expeditions, and Wadi el-Hol's debated inscriptions.
Introduces acrophony, Serabit el-Khadim, Wadi el-Hol, the bʿlt proposal, and the competing dates and readings.
Follows the better-attested alphabetic branches and distinguishes Ugaritic cuneiform from the Phoenician line.
Returns the alphabet story to scribal institutions, administration, restricted literacy, and the different work scripts performed.
Offers a practical cross-reference for reading signs as image, sound, category, and context together.

leavesOut: This collection does not claim that Egyptians used an exclusive alphabet, that every Proto-Sinaitic reading is secure, or that Egyptian writing is a simple direct ancestor of every later alphabet.

title: Egypt and the Abrahamic traditions
blurb: A layered route through documented influence, Jewish life in Egypt, Islamic tradition, Christian memory, and the problem of later judgment parallels.
purpose: To distinguish Egyptian evidence, biblical literature, Jewish and Christian reception, Islamic tradition, and modern theory while asking when resemblance becomes a defensible influence claim.

steps.why: Establishes the archive's four-layer boundary and rejects the Moses–Akhenaten identification as unproven modern theory.
Tests the Amenemope–Proverbs case against weaker hymn, love-poetry, and genre parallels.
Uses Aramaic papyri to place a Judaean garrison community inside Egyptian legal and religious life.
Treats Yusuf, Musa, Firʿawn, Muslim scholarship, medieval antiquarianism, and Coptic–Muslim history as a distinct Islamic cluster.
Follows Coptic, Arabic, and Islamic engagements with Egyptian language, places, institutions, and later memory.
Applies resemblance-versus-transmission reasoning to the weighing of the heart, judgment, resurrection, and moral accounting.
Returns to the evidence ladder, alphabet-origin claims, parallelomania, and the archive's responsibility to preserve uncertainty.

leavesOut: This collection does not harmonize Egyptian, Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions into one origin story, settle the historicity of Exodus, or infer transmission from resemblance alone.
